analysis.one_liner: Blocks the FCC from creating low-power community FM radio stations.
analysis.headline: The bill to block new low-power FM community radio stations died in the Senate Commerce Committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The FCC had proposed letting churches, schools, and community groups run tiny 10- to 100-watt FM radio stations in their own neighborhoods. This bill would have forbidden the FCC from creating that service at all, cancelled any low-power rules already issued, and voided any licenses already granted. It was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee and never received a vote, so it never became law.
analysis.who_benefits: Existing full-power FM radio stations would benefit: they would face no new tiny competitors on the dial, and no risk of interference from neighboring low-power transmitters. Larger station owners had argued low-power stations could disrupt their signals. The public would gain nothing new, since the bill created nothing and only removed a service the FCC had proposed for community groups.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would have barred the FCC entirely from creating the low-power FM service it had proposed in Docket No. 99-25, and would have terminated any rules already issued and voided any low-power licenses already granted.
It did this by overriding the FCC's normal authority under section 303 of the Communications Act to regulate the radio spectrum, reserving that decision to Congress instead.

analysis.who_pays: Community groups, churches, schools, and neighborhood organizations that wanted to broadcast to their own blocks would bear the cost: the bill voided any licenses already issued and foreclosed the service entirely. Ordinary listeners would lose a potential source of local, noncommercial programming.
analysis.who_pays_short: Community groups wanting local radio stations

drawbacks.text: The bill would have voided any low-power FM licenses already issued under FCC rules, taking stations away from community operators who had received them.
Its stated purpose was protecting existing full-power stations from interference from new low-power neighbors, a real concern for listeners that broadcasters argued the FCC's plan underestimated.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's stated rationale was preventing interference with existing full-power stations, but its cost would have been the loss of a new, very inexpensive way for community groups, churches, and schools to serve their own neighborhoods on the public airwaves. It offered no benefit to ordinary listeners beyond protection against a form of interference the FCC's proposal was already designed to limit, so its drawbacks outweighed any gain. The bill never became law, so no such cost was imposed.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate introduced the bill and sent it to the Commerce Committee, which never voted on it, and it died when the 106th Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 10, 2000, read twice, and referred to the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.
No further action was ever taken: it never left committee, never received a floor vote in the Senate, and was never taken up by the House.

Had it become law, it would have prohibited the FCC from creating the low-power FM radio service it had proposed, terminated any rules already issued, and voided any low-power licenses already granted.
The bill died when the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Community groups seeking low-power radio licenses were better off, since the FCC's new service was not blocked. Full-power broadcasters failed to stop it by legislation, though they later won restrictions on the service through other means.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Community groups seeking low-power FM licenses

for.name: Sen. Judd Gregg
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on February 10, 2000, and gave introductory remarks.

for.name: 35 Senate cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors of the bill.

for.name: National Association of Broadcasters
for.role: Trade association of full-power radio and TV stations
for.what_they_did: Lobbied Congress to block the FCC's low-power FM service, arguing it would interfere with existing stations.

against.name: Federal Communications Commission
against.what_they_did: Had proposed the low-power FM service (Docket No. 99-25) that the bill would have prohibited, and opposed legislation shutting it down.

against.name: Community media and public-interest groups
against.what_they_did: Publicly backed the FCC's low-power FM proposal and opposed bills like this one that would block it.

sides.party_line_note: Of the 36 senators behind the bill, 30 were Republicans and 5 were Democrats, so support skewed heavily toward one party but was not unanimous on either side.

industries.industry: Full-power commercial and public radio broadcasters
industries.note: The bill would have eliminated a new class of tiny competitors for listeners and dial space, locking in the existing stations' hold on the FM band. Because the bill died, broadcasters gained nothing.

industries.industry: Low-power FM applicants (community groups, churches, schools)
industries.note: The bill would have shut them out of the airwaves entirely and voided any licenses already issued. It failed, and the service went ahead, though its final scope was narrowed by other legislation later in 2000.
